topics.chapterTitle: Designing Asynchronous C++ Execution and Coroutine Lifetimes
topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A synchronous function’s stack often makes lifetime look simple: the caller waits while the callee uses its arguments. An asynchronous operation separates initiation from completion. The initiating function may return while a buffer is still being read, a callback is queued, or a coroutine is suspended. The algorithm may be correct while the ownership around it is not.

topics.title: 5.1.1 Understanding Operation State and Completion Handlers
topics.summary: An asynchronous operation needs state that survives initiation. That state may include a socket, a buffer, a deadline, a decoder position, a callback, and an error result. If any of these are local variables in a function that returns before completion, the operation must either own them elsewhere or retain a valid reference under a documented lifetime rule.

blocks.text: Think of initiation as creating a pending obligation. Completion settles that obligation with a result, error, or cancellation outcome. The caller needs to know whether initiation itself can fail before the obligation exists. Otherwise it may wait for a callback that will never arrive or destroy state while a callback remains possible.

blocks.text: A useful interface states whether a successfully initiated operation invokes its completion exactly once and whether completion may occur inline. Inline completion can reenter caller code before the initiating function finishes updating its own state. Deferring every handler can simplify some reasoning but adds queueing and does not automatically remove races.

topics.chapterTitle: Designing Asynchronous C++ Execution and Coroutine Lifetimes
topics.title: 5.1.2 Choosing Execution Contexts and Serialization Rules
topics.summary: An executor determines where work is submitted; an execution context supplies machinery that runs it. These terms do not imply one thread per operation. A single event loop can interleave many waiting operations, while a thread pool can run ready handlers concurrently. The correct choice depends on work duration, blocking behavior, and ownership of shared state.

blocks.text: A strand in Boost.Asio provides a serialization guarantee for associated handlers; it does not necessarily pin them to one operating-system thread. Thread-local state and thread affinity therefore need separate reasoning. A component can be race-free under a strand while still being wrong if it assumes all calls occur on one specific thread. (R04)

topics.chapterTitle: Designing Asynchronous C++ Execution and Coroutine Lifetimes
topics.title: 5.2.1 Distinguishing Suspension from Parallel Execution
topics.summary: A coroutine can suspend and later resume while preserving execution state. Suspension does not itself create a thread, schedule I/O, or guarantee parallel execution. The awaiter and surrounding runtime determine when and where resumption occurs. A program using co_await can still block, deadlock, or execute entirely on one thread.

topics.title: 5.2.2 Preserving Owned Data Across Suspension
topics.summary: Passing an object by value into a coroutine can place an owned copy or moved value in the frame. Passing a reference stores a reference-like relationship; it does not extend the referred object’s lifetime. A coroutine parameter of std::string_view still borrows storage even though the coroutine itself remains alive.

topics.title: 5.3.1 Distinguishing Stop Requests from Resource Reclamation
topics.summary: A cancellation request says that continuing the operation is no longer desired under the relevant policy. It does not prove that execution has stopped at that instant. A handler may already be running, a kernel operation may be pending, or a remote service may have committed. Resource reclamation must wait for the point that the actual API defines as completion or safe cancellation.

topics.title: 5.3.2 Keeping Child Work Within an Owned Scope
topics.summary: Structured concurrency is the design goal that spawned work has an explicit owning scope and does not escape silently. Before the scope ends, its child operations are completed, cancelled and joined, or transferred to another named owner. This makes cleanup and error propagation easier to reason about than detached tasks with implicit lifetimes.

blocks.text: Cancellation must establish what happens to the callback registration and its target. One design keeps shared operation state alive until the transport confirms that no callback can occur. Another removes the registration under the transport’s supported cancellation protocol and waits for completion ownership to settle. The correct choice depends on the executor and library contract, not on the presence of co_await syntax.

blocks.text: An operation state machine might distinguish registered, completing, cancelled-awaiting-transport, and released. Exactly one path owns the final transition that releases resources. A cancellation flag can influence the result delivered to the caller, but the transport still owns its pending callback until the protocol says otherwise.

blocks.text: Do not solve the problem by making every object globally shared without a lifetime plan. Shared ownership can prevent early destruction while creating cycles or retaining a large request graph indefinitely. Use explicit ownership for the operation state, and break callback links when the completion protocol permits it.

blocks.text: Solution reasoning. Both early destruction and normal completion must release frame-owned objects once. An initiation failure before ownership transfer leaves cleanup with the caller. A successfully initiated borrowed operation must settle its lifetime obligation even when cancellation is requested. A coroutine’s existence is not proof that a borrowed object is alive, and a stop request is not proof that a handler has stopped using it.

reading.title: Practice and implementation lab
paragraphs: Add a third stage that owns a vector of input values and computes a bounded sum. Destroy one task after the first stage and allow another to finish. Instrument a small RAII object inside the coroutine to verify cleanup in both cases. Keep the trace deterministic and avoid measuring timing as a substitute for checking destruction.

Next, design an asynchronous submission interface on paper. State who owns the payload, whether completion can run inline, where it runs, how cancellation is requested, and which event permits buffer reuse. Describe what happens if initiation throws before the operation is registered.

Solution reasoning. Both early destruction and normal completion must release frame-owned objects once. An initiation failure before ownership transfer leaves cleanup with the caller. A successfully initiated borrowed operation must settle its lifetime obligation even when cancellation is requested. A coroutine’s existence is not proof that a borrowed object is alive, and a stop request is not proof that a handler has stopped using it.
Chapter takeaway. Asynchronous syntax changes control flow; explicit ownership and completion rules make that control flow safe.
